A prerequisite for elimination is knowing that multiplying both sides of an equation by the same nonzero number gives an equivalent equation.

Add the equations when a variable's coefficients are opposites; subtract when they are equal; if neither happens, multiply one or both equations by a nonzero constant first so that one variable's coefficients become opposites.
Step 1: write both equations in standard form, one under the other, with x-terms above x-terms and y-terms above y-terms; 2x + 3y = 12 sits directly above 5x - 3y = 9.
The elimination procedure for the system 2x + 3y = 12 and 5x - 3y = 9 has six steps, in this order.
Step 2: compare the coefficients of x and of y; if one pair is opposite, add, and if one pair is equal, subtract; the y-coefficients +3 and -3 are opposites, so add.

Step 3: if no pair cancels, multiply one or both equations by a nonzero constant so that one variable's coefficients become opposites, multiplying every term including the constant; for 2x + 3y = 12 and 4x + y = 10 you could multiply the first equation by -2.

rows.text: Step 4: combine the two equations term by term; the chosen variable's terms cancel to zero, leaving one equation in one variable; (2x + 3y) + (5x - 3y) = 12 + 9 gives 7x = 21.
Step 5: solve the one-variable equation, then put that value into either original equation to find the other variable; x = 3, so 2(3) + 3y = 12 gives 3y = 6 and y = 2.
Step 6: write the solution as an ordered pair and substitute it into both original equations to confirm; (3, 2) checks because 2(3) + 3(2) = 12 and 5(3) - 3(2) = 9 both hold.

rows.text: When you multiply an equation by a constant, every term must be multiplied, including the constant on the right; leaving the constant alone changes the equation into a different one with a different solution.
Multiplying 2x + 3y = 7 by 2 incorrectly as 4x + 6y = 7 is wrong; the correct result is 4x + 6y = 14.

If a variable's coefficients are equal and have the same sign, adding them gives twice the variable, not zero; subtract instead, and subtract every term on both sides.

Subtracting the second equation from the first in 3x + 4y = 10 and 3x - y = 5 gives (3x - 3x) + (4y - (-y)) = 10 - 5.

rows.text: A sentence's pattern is a choice about what the reader gets first, and what the reader gets first is what they feel most.
Every sentence needs a subject and a verb, and that unit is called a main clause (or independent clause).
Words that add detail — phrases and describing clauses — are called modifiers.
When two clauses or phrases share the same grammatical shape, the sentence is parallel.
A pattern is not grammar-correct vs. incorrect; all three patterns are correct, but each creates a different rhythm and emphasis.
In a periodic sentence, modifiers and setup come first and the main clause waits until the very end, so the reader hangs on every word.
The effect of a periodic sentence is suspense and a strong final punch, and the reader cannot relax until the sentence finishes.

source.title: periodic sentence
source.quote: in order to create the effect of anticipation or suspense

rows.text: The effect of a cumulative sentence is a clear, immediate point plus richness: the reader gets the news right away, then gets the texture.
In a cumulative sentence, the main clause opens the sentence and modifiers are added on afterward like freight cars behind the engine.
Neither the periodic nor the cumulative pattern is better: periodic builds suspense and lands the point at the end, while cumulative leads with the point and lets the detail pile up.
In a balanced sentence both halves have the same shape: subject + verb + object.
In a balanced sentence the reader hears the first half, then expects — and gets — the echo.
In a balanced sentence there is equal weight on both halves, which is why it feels fair and finished.
To balance a sentence, rewrite each half in the same grammatical shape, then let the second half mirror the first.
A main clause is a group of words with its own subject and verb that could stand alone as a complete sentence, and it is the one the sentence is really about.
Modifiers are words or phrases that add description or detail but cannot stand alone, like "worn out but stubborn" or "in the last minute."
Modifiers dress up the sentence; they are not the sentence's spine.
An independent clause is a clause with a subject and a verb that expresses a complete thought and can be a sentence by itself.
If a clause starts with a word like "because," "when," or "although," it cannot stand alone.
Parallelism is repeating the same grammatical shape in two or more parts of a sentence, so the parts mirror each other.
Periodic sentences delay the main clause; cumulative sentences lead with it and keep adding; balanced sentences mirror two equal ideas.
The answer to matching "Exhausted, nervous, and out of time, Marcus finally handed in his essay." to its pattern is Periodic.

A fragment is missing a subject or a verb — it is not a complete sentence, even if it sounds stylish; the fix is to add a subject or verb, or attach it to a nearby complete sentence.

rows.text: Six punctuation marks (dash, colon, semicolon, comma, period, ellipsis) can reshape a sentence.
Dashes, colons, and semicolons are not decoration — each one tells the reader how long to pause and what to pay attention to.
A dash creates an abrupt, dramatic pause, like slamming on the brakes to make the reader notice what comes next.
A colon signals 'here it comes': it announces an explanation, a list, or a payoff after a complete sentence.
A semicolon joins two closely related complete sentences into one thought, tighter than a period but stronger than a comma.

source.title: Semicolon
source.quote: a semicolon is most commonly used to link (in a single sentence) two independent clauses that are closely related in thought

rows.text: A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences, and that error is called a comma splice.

rows.text: The dash is a dramatic brake: an abrupt, sharp pause that yanks the reader forward and puts spotlight emphasis on whatever comes after it.
The colon follows a complete sentence and announces that a payoff — an explanation or list — is arriving next.
The semicolon welds two closely related complete sentences into one, keeping their connection tight without a full stop.

rows.text: Punctuation is sound made visible — you can hear it before you can name it.

rows.text: A comma is a light pause inside a sentence, or it separates items in a list.

The rook moves only along straight lines — up, down, left or right — and can travel any distance in one move; diagonals and jumping are not rook moves.

source.title: Chesquerque
source.quote: On a point with diagonals, though, a rook can also move one step diagonally.

rows.text: The answer to rolling the rook up the d-file as far as it can go is Rd5.
The answer to finding the rook's capture is Rxd7.
The rook rolls straight up from d4 through d5, but the white pawn on d6 blocks the lane, so d5 is the farthest square it can reach.
Rolling straight up the d-file, the first piece the rook meets is the black pawn on d7, so it stops on that square and captures it.
The answer to which move a rook on c3 is not allowed to make is rook to f6.
From c3, the squares c6, g3 and a3 all sit on straight lines (same file or same row), but f6 is on a slanted diagonal, and the rook never moves diagonally.
